title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 110
paragraphs: After hearing this and taking up the child, the herdsman went back by the way he had come and arrived at his dwelling. Now his own wife, who had been on the point of giving birth every day, by a providential chance delivered her child at just this time, while her husband was away in the city. Both were in anxiety, each for the other: the man afraid about his wife's labor, the woman about why Harpagos had summoned her husband so urgently, which he had never done before. So as soon as he came back and stood before her, his wife, seeing him again beyond her hopes, was the first to speak, and asked him for what purpose Harpagos had sent for him. He answered: “Wife, when I came to the city I saw and heard things I wish I had never seen, and which I wish had never befallen those whom we serve. The whole house of Harpagos was full of mourning, and in my astonishment I went inside. As soon as I entered I saw laid out to view an infant child gasping for breath and screaming, which was adorned with gold ornaments and embroidered clothing. When Harpagos saw me he ordered me at once to take up the child and carry it away and lay it on that part of the mountains most haunted by wild beasts, saying that Astyages had laid this task upon me, and threatening me with many punishments if I failed. I took the child and carried it off, supposing it was the son of one of the servants of the house, for I could never have guessed whose child it really was. But I marveled to see it adorned with gold and fine raiment, and I marveled too that mourning was made for it openly in the house of Harpagos. And straightaway on the road I learned the whole matter from the servant who came with me out of the city and placed the babe in my hands: namely that it was in truth the son of Mandane, the daughter of Astyages, and of Cambyses the son of Cyrus, and that Astyages orders it to be killed. And now here it is.”
